---
title: "Filing bug reports"
---

When something doesn't render the way you expected, a good bug report
makes the difference between "fixed in an hour" and "back-and-forth
for a week." Most of the time we need three things:

1. A small `.qmd` file that reproduces the problem.
2. The exact `quarto` command you ran.
3. Either the rendered output (HTML, PDF, …) or the error message.

If those three things are enough, you're done — open an issue at
<https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2/issues> and attach them.

## Attach a pipeline trace when you can

For anything beyond a trivial parse error — a transform that misbehaves,
crossrefs that don't resolve, a sidebar that comes out empty, a
website-stage that produces unexpected HTML — please attach a
**pipeline trace.** A trace captures the document at every internal
stage of the render, so we can see exactly where things went off the
rails without having to recreate your environment.

To generate one, add `trace: true` to your document's YAML frontmatter:

```yaml
---
title: "My doc"
trace: true
---
```

Render the document normally:

```bash
quarto render my-doc.qmd
```

The trace will be written to:

```
.quarto/trace/my-doc/latest.json.gz
```

Attach that file to your issue. It's gzipped and typically well under
1 MB even for medium-sized documents — small enough to drop directly
into a GitHub comment.

## What's in a trace, and what isn't

A trace contains:

- The pipeline stages that ran and their order.
- An AST snapshot at each stage boundary.
- Stage timings (so we can spot regressions).
- The git hash of the `quarto` build that produced the trace.
- The path to your input document and your output document.

A trace does **not** contain:

- The contents of your input `.qmd` file (we still need that
  separately — the trace records the parsed AST, not the raw
  Markdown).
- Files referenced by your document (images, includes, bibliographies,
  etc.). If the bug involves one of those, attach it too.
- Anything from outside the document — environment variables, your
  shell history, files elsewhere on your machine.

The AST snapshots include text content from your document, so if your
document is sensitive, treat the trace as you'd treat the document.

## Inspecting a trace yourself

You don't have to know what's in a trace to file a useful bug report,
but if you want to look:

```bash
# List traces in the current project
quarto trace list

# Print a single stage's snapshot (pretty-printed)
quarto trace show --doc my-doc --stage parse

# Open the interactive viewer in a browser
quarto trace view
```

The on-disk format is gzipped JSON; if you want raw bytes for `jq` or
similar, decompress first:

```bash
gunzip -c .quarto/trace/my-doc/latest.json.gz | jq .schema_version
```
